summary: Records the process and findings of the CAPWAP working group's evaluation team, which reviewed the four candidate protocols submitted to the working group on 26 June 2005. It is an informational record rather than a protocol specification.

plainLanguage.summary: Four teams offered ideas for how to control Wi-Fi boxes. A review team compared them and wrote down what they found.

which protocol was chosen for capwap control
subtitle: How four candidate protocols were evaluated for controlling Wi-Fi access points

tldr.problem: The CAPWAP working group needed to select a protocol for controlling and provisioning wireless access points, and four candidate protocols were submitted for evaluation.
tldr.mechanism: An evaluation team reviewed LWAPP, SLAPP, CTP, and WiCoP against 15 mandatory and 5 desirable objectives covering architecture, security, interoperability and other requirements.
tldr.outcome: LWAPP was recommended as the basis for the CAPWAP protocol, with suggested enhancements drawn from the other proposals, particularly in areas like security and data tunneling modes.

today: RFC 4565 is an informational record of the CAPWAP evaluation process. It guided the working group in developing RFC 5415, which standardized the CAPWAP protocol based primarily on LWAPP with enhancements.

sections.title: Introduction and Evaluation Process
sections.content:
The Control and Provisioning of Wireless Access Points (CAPWAP) Working Group received four candidate protocols for controlling access points: LWAPP (Light Weight Access Point Protocol), SLAPP (Secure Light Access Point Protocol), CTP (CAPWAP Tunneling Protocol), and WiCoP (Wireless LAN Control Protocol). An evaluation team was formed to assess each proposal against the working group objectives.

The evaluation used a systematic process inspired by earlier IETF evaluations. Two evaluators were assigned to each protocol: one writing a favorable assessment and one using strict criteria. Each objective was rated as Failure (F), Partial (P), or Compliant (C). The team held teleconferences to discuss the briefs and deliver team ratings.
sections.plainLanguage: Four teams offered ideas and a group of experts reviewed each one fairly, with one person trying to like it and another being strict. They rated each idea on whether it solved the main goals.

sections.title: The Four Candidate Protocols
sections.content:
LWAPP is the most detailed proposal. It focuses on 802.11 WLAN monitoring and configuration, using raw 802.11 frames tunneled back to the Access Controller (AC). It supports both local-MAC mode (where the WTP handles user data forwarding) and split-MAC mode (where the AC processes frames).

SLAPP distinguishes itself with established technologies: Generic Routing Encapsulation (GRE) for user data tunneling and Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) for control channel security. It supports four modes of operation combining local-MAC and split-MAC architectures.

CTP uses Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) to define configuration and management data. It was designed to support multiple wireless technologies, not just 802.11. It defines separate packet frame types for control and data messages.

WiCoP introduces new discovery, configuration and management mechanisms. It proposes using standard security and authentication methods such as IPsec and EAP, and defines 802.11 Quality of Service parameters.
sections.plainLanguage: LWAPP sends 802.11 frames to a central controller. SLAPP uses GRE tunneling and standard DTLS security. CTP leverages SNMP for management. WiCoP proposes IPsec and EAP for security.

sections.title: Security and Protocol Strength
sections.content:
The evaluation team assessed protocol security but noted that this team was not a security team and any resulting CAPWAP protocol would need to undergo full IETF security review. LWAPP received a Compliant rating for protocol security with the note that it has undergone one third-party security review. SLAPP is compliant because it wraps control and management in DTLS, which is an established standard.

CTP and WiCoP both failed the protocol security objective. CTP fails because it does not perform explicit mutual authentication and does not mutually derive session keys. WiCoP fails because there is not enough specific information to implement its security features using EAP and IPsec.

The evaluation team recommended that whatever security protocol is specified for CAPWAP, its use cases must be described in detail with at least one mandatory authentication and cipher method, and suggested DTLS as a standards-based alternative to LWAPP's proprietary security mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: LWAPP and SLAPP use proven security methods. CTP and WiCoP didn't explain their security well enough. The team said CAPWAP should either use DTLS (which is standard) or clearly explain how it does security.

sections.title: Mandatory Objectives Results
sections.content:
The evaluation assessed 15 mandatory objectives covering logical groups, traffic separation, STA transparency, configuration consistency, firmware triggers, resource monitoring, QoS control, security, IEEE 802.11i support, interoperability, specification completeness, vendor independence, vendor flexibility, and NAT traversal.

All four protocols achieved Compliant on most objectives: logical groups, STA transparency, configuration consistency, and interoperability were fully met by all four. LWAPP scored highest overall with 11 Compliant ratings. SLAPP achieved 9 Compliant ratings. CTP and WiCoP each achieved 7 Compliant ratings but both failed on protocol security and system-wide security, and both partially failed on resource control and traffic separation.

The evaluation team identified that LWAPP's main weakness was limited support for local-MAC mode data tunneling, while CTP and WiCoP needed more detailed security specifications and complete protocol definitions.
sections.plainLanguage: All four handled Wi-Fi groups and addressing well. LWAPP was strongest overall. CTP and WiCoP had security and specification gaps that needed fixing.

sections.title: Evaluation Conclusions and Recommendations
sections.content:
The evaluation team concluded that LWAPP should be used as the basis for the CAPWAP protocol because it is the most complete base protocol and flexible enough to be extended or modified by the working group. However, the team recommended incorporating enhancements from the other proposals.

High-priority recommendations included: expanding LWAPP's information elements field from 8 bits to support more attributes; adopting a standards-based security protocol like DTLS instead of LWAPP's proprietary security; supporting local-MAC mode data tunneling by tunneling user data as 802.3 Ethernet frames; and ensuring the protocol can negotiate which tunneling modes are supported.

Additional recommendations suggested removing LWAPP's redundant Layer 2 encapsulation for data tunneling, using standard protocols like GRE or L2TP for user data encapsulation, and abstracting STA access control outside the 802.11 binding to support future wireless technologies.
sections.plainLanguage: The team picked LWAPP as the starting point but said to borrow ideas from the others: use standard DTLS security, support more tunneling modes, and make it work with non-802.11 wireless systems.
